title: Bitcoin Could Be Entering a New Bull Market Despite Latest Sell-Off
summary: BloFin Research says Bitcoin's new bull market remains intact despite the latest sell-off, as historical data suggests its boom-and-bust cycles are weakening.
content:
Despite the market dip and liquidations over the past week, Bitcoin has seemingly entered a bull market, as the analysis of its 50-week moving average shows.

BloFin Research argues that Bitcoin's traditional four-year boom-and-bust cycle is gradually losing strength. Future rallies could deliver smaller gains, followed by shorter and less severe downturns.

The strongest evidence comes from Bitcoin's recovery above its 50-week moving average, a technical indicator that previously signaled bull-market transitions in 2015, 2019 and 2023.

Bitcoin reclaimed this level near $78,800 in September. It subsequently traded above $86,000 in early October.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin's MVRV ratio, which compares its current market value with the average price investors paid for their coins, moved above its annual average.

As of October 11, MVRV stood near 1.54, above its 365-day average of 1.44. This suggests the longer-term recovery remains intact despite recent selling.

It means Bitcoin's market strength is improving, a signal that has previously appeared during the early stages of bull markets.

BloFin's most significant finding concerns the declining severity of Bitcoin's market cycles.

Bitcoin fell approximately 53% from its October 2025 peak of $124,824 to $58,525 in June 2026.

Previous bear markets were considerably worse:

Bear market

Peak-to-trough decline

2013–2015

84.5%

2017–2018

83.8%

2021–2022

76.7%

2025–2026

53%

Bull-market gains have also narrowed. Bitcoin's trough-to-peak returns have declined from roughly 530 times in its earliest cycle to eight times in the most recent one.

If June remains the bottom, the latest bear market lasted approximately eight months, compared with 12–13 months historically.

BloFin Research attributes much of this change to longer-term ownership. In September, approximately 16.64 million BTC, or 83% of circulating supply, had remained unmoved for at least 155 days.

Meanwhile, US spot Bitcoin ETFs held around 1.3 million BTC on October 2. Public companies owned another 1.29 million BTC.

Together, ETFs and corporate treasuries controlled approximately 13% of circulating Bitcoin.

However, last week's $679 million ETF outflow shows that institutional demand can still weaken sharply during market stress.

Bitcoin was trading around $83,000 on October 11, still above the September moving-average breakout level and well above its June low.

The four-year cycle also remains visible. Bitcoin peaked roughly 18 months after the April 2024 halving, consistent with historical patterns.

For traders, a sustained move below the current 50-week moving average would weaken the bullish signal. A break beneath $58,525 would challenge the proposed cycle bottom.

For now, Bitcoin's longer-term recovery indicators remain positive. The recent ETF withdrawals show why the transition toward a more stable market could still involve sharp corrections.

Read the Original story Bitcoin Could Be Entering a New Bull Market Despite Latest Sell-Off by BloFin Research at beincrypto.com

summary: Bitcoin opened at $83,673.01 on Monday, October 12, 2026, up 0.9% from Sunday's opening price. As of 7:25 a.m. ET this morning, bitcoin dipped to $83,280.11. Ethereum opened at $2,534.30, up 1.2% from Sunday's opening price. The price of ethereum moved slightly higher this morning to $2,543.06 as of 7:25 a.m. ET.
content:
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) opened at $83,673.01 on Monday, October 12, 2026 , up 0.9% from Sunday's opening price. As of 7:25 a.m. ET this morning, bitcoin dipped to $83,280.11.

Ethereum ( ETH-USD ) opened at $2,534.30 on Monday, October 12, 2026 , up 1.2% from Sunday's opening price. The price of ethereum moved slightly higher this morning to $2,543.06 as of 7:25 a.m. ET.

Bitcoin and ethereum prices have regained some ground from lower opening prices on Friday, and are generally back in line with where prices opened last Thursday.

The same forces that drove crypto prices lower toward the end of last week are still firmly in play this week, including the ever-growing AI bubble, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and Treasury yields hitting historic highs.

Here's more on how bond yields "threaten" crypto prices:

US Treasury bonds offer investors regular interest payments backed by the government. When their yields rise, investors can earn higher returns without taking the same risks associated with cryptocurrencies.

Bitcoin pays no fixed interest. As a result, higher Treasury yields can encourage investors to move capital into government bonds or hold cash.

Bitunix argues that this shift in investor preferences is creating additional pressure on Bitcoin and other speculative assets.

The risk extends beyond crypto. Higher yields also increase borrowing costs and can reduce the appeal of technology stocks. Bitunix reported weekly declines in crypto-linked equities, including Strategy and Circle.

Keep reading: Bitcoin's Next Move Depends on the US Bond Market and Inflation Report

Bitcoin's price this morning, Monday, October 12, 2026 , was up 0.9% from Sunday's opening price. Here's a look at how the opening bitcoin price has changed versus last week, month, and year:

One week ago: -3.2%

One month ago: +8.4%

One year ago: -24.5%

The all-time high for bitcoin was $126,198.07 on Oct. 6, 2025. The all-time low value for bitcoin was $0.04865 on July 14, 2010.

The price of ethereum this morning, Monday, October 12, 2026, was 1.2% higher than Sunday's open. Here's a look at how the opening ethereum price has changed versus last week, month, and year:

One week ago: -7.1%

One month ago: +0.8%

One year ago: -32.4%

The all-time high for ethereum was $4,953.73 on Aug. 24, 2025. The all-time low value for ethereum was $0.4209 on Oct. 21, 2015.

Bitcoin, ethereum, and other cryptocurrencies are rapidly evolving. Follow the latest developments from Yahoo Finance and others here .

Bitcoin is a type of cryptocurrency, which is a currency that exists only in digital form and operates without government or banking oversight. By comparison, the U.S. dollar, the EU euro, the Canadian dollar, and other national currencies have paper versions and are issued by their respective governments.

Bitcoin relies on a public digital ledger that validates and records transactions and verifies bitcoin ownership. This ledger is called the blockchain, and it is globally distributed — that is, decentralized — across a broad, worldwide network of servers.

Decentralization is a fundamental aspect of cryptocurrencies. Decentralization facilitates peer-to-peer payments with no banking intermediary, enhanced security, and defense against manipulation attempts.

Learn more: What is Bitcoin, and how does it work?

There are several ways to buy Bitcoin. You can go through a crypto exchange, a fintech app, or a traditional brokerage that will allow you to buy into a bitcoin ETF.

Before placing a trade, though, decide what you actually want: full ownership of your bitcoin and private keys — or easy price exposure inside a familiar, regulated system.

Whichever avenue you take, it's important to remember that bitcoin remains a high-risk, highly volatile asset compared to many other investments. Prices can surge or drop quickly, sometimes without warning. If you're considering buying bitcoin, assume volatility is part of the deal.

title: AI Price Prediction: Insights from Grok on Bitcoin’s Potential by Election Day
summary: Grok crunched Bitcoin's price structure, fund flows, and midterm election history to land on a specific target for November 3. Whether its forecast holds depends on two price zones every Bitcoin holder should know right now.
content:
Grok forecasts Bitcoin closes around $85,000 on November 3 midterm election day, just above its current $82,940 price.

Grok assigns a 30% chance Bitcoin exceeds $90,000 and a 25% chance it drops below $75,000 by election day.

Election results could swing Bitcoin 7% in either direction within a week, with congressional control influencing key crypto legislation.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Grok, the AI chatbot developed by xAI, expects that Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) could close around $85,000 on November 3, 2026, the day of the U.S. midterm elections. This forecast is only slightly above Bitcoin's current price of about $82,940, as of October 11.

Bitcoin has dipped 2.7% in the past week but gained 7.4% over the last month. In just two weeks, it hit a high of $87,249 on October 2, then fell to $80,000 on October 8. So, how did Grok arrive at the $85,000 target, and how much weight should Bitcoin holders give it?

Before we asked our question, we gave Grok some relevant data. At the time, Bitcoin was trading at $83,007, roughly a year after it hit an all-time high of $126,080 on October 6, 2025. The lowest point since then was on June 30, when it fell to $57,717.

Since then, Bitcoin has made higher lows, suggesting each pullback has stopped above the last, with buyers stepping in around the mid-$70,000s in September and again at $80,000 on October 8. On that date, exchanges had to close $1.1 billion worth of leveraged positions—trades made with borrowed funds that exchanges close once losses eat through the trader's deposit.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

------

We also shared information about Bitcoin funds. Spot Bitcoin funds, which directly hold Bitcoin for investors who buy shares through brokerage accounts, have a total of $105.8 billion in assets. These funds saw a $731 million outflow on October 7 and 8, but investors added $21 million on October 9.

Finally, we included historical election data, noting that Bitcoin fell about 20% in the month leading up to the 2022 midterms, largely due to the collapse of a major crypto exchange, and dropped about 7% in the four weeks before the 2018 midterms.

Grok believes Bitcoin is consolidating, trading in a relatively narrow range while maintaining its pattern of higher lows. It also considered the short-term holder cost basis—the average price recent buyers paid—which Grok assessed at the low-to-mid $70,000s. This price point matters because traders often watch it, knowing newer buyers might sell if prices fall below what they paid.

According to Grok, the price structure remains positive as long as Bitcoin stays above this support zone. It identified resistance, where selling typically occurs, in the mid-to-high $80,000s. Grok's main scenario suggests a slow upward trend, tempered by caution ahead of the elections and the historical trend of weak fourth quarters during midterm years. However, it noted the uncertainty of this trend, as past cycle bottoms and the 2022 exchange failure complicate the picture.

Volatility is a key reason Grok maintains its close-to-current price forecast. Options traders gauge implied volatility, or expected price movement, using contracts that let them buy or sell in the future at a set price. Grok noted a reading in the mid-30s, signifying a probable swing of around 8% to 9% in the three weeks before the elections.

Grok provided an 80% confidence range for Bitcoin's price on November 3, estimating it between $72,000 and $97,000. The lower end of this range reflects a possible test of short-term holder support, while the upper end suggests a potential breakout above recent highs.

Additionally, Grok assigned a 30% chance of Bitcoin exceeding $90,000 on November 3, and a 25% chance of it dropping below $75,000. This assessment leans slightly to the upside, tempered by election-related uncertainties and recent fund outflows.

We inquired whether the election outcome could influence Bitcoin's price. Grok confirmed it could, expecting a potential price move of about 7% in either direction within a week after the election, depending on how the results align with investor expectations. Control of Congress can also affect key crypto legislation, such as the stalled CLARITY Act. Historically, Bitcoin's price reactions after elections have varied, though it often trends positively over more extended periods.

Grok formulated its forecasts based on the data we provided, without access to live buy and sell orders on exchanges. The model also independently calculated the probabilities rather than reading them from any market.

We consider Grok's $85,000 estimate a reasonable midpoint for this three-week forecast, mainly because volatility metrics suggest limited room for significant movement in either direction. Bitcoin holders should watch two key areas: a close above Grok's resistance in the mid-to-high $80,000s could validate its more optimistic scenarios, while a drop below the low-to-mid $70,000s could bring the $72,000 lower boundary into play.

Monitoring fund flows provides an additional gauge. After the $731 million outflow from Bitcoin funds on October 7 and 8, steady inflows could help support the upward move Grok described. Ultimately, Bitcoin's price on November 3 will put Grok's model to the test.

title: Bitcoin struggles above $83,000 a year after $19 billion crypto crash
summary: Investing.com -- Bitcoin remained above $83,000 on Sunday, roughly 34% below its record high, as investors marked one year since a historic $19 billion cryptocurrency liquidation event.
content:
Investing.com -- Bitcoin remained above $83,000 on Sunday, roughly 34% below its record high, as investors marked one year since a historic $19 billion cryptocurrency liquidation event.

Before you buy NVIDIA: our AI model's stock picks are beating the market by 120%+. See the list now »

The world's largest cryptocurrency was trading at $83,062.8 as at 01:23 ET (05:23 GMT), having failed to recover its October 6, 2025, peak of $126,080.

The anniversary follows another volatile week in which Bitcoin fell to $80,308 before recovering towards $83,000, highlighting persistent concerns over leveraged trading.

On October 10, 2025, Bitcoin plunged from approximately $122,000 to $105,000 after President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs on Chinese imports.

The selloff triggered more than $19 billion in liquidations across cryptocurrency markets, affecting approximately 1.6 million trading accounts.

Analysts warn that the conditions behind the crash remain largely intact, particularly the widespread use of perpetual futures and heavily leveraged positions.

Mark Connors of Risk Dimensions said derivatives positioning continues to influence Bitcoin's short-term price movements, despite improvements in market transparency.

Recent positioning data suggests approximately $3.3 billion in Bitcoin short positions could face liquidation if prices climb towards $85,000, potentially accelerating any recovery.

Institutional demand has also weakened, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recording more than $700 million in outflows this week.

Despite the market's struggles, Bitwise Asset Management Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan remains optimistic about Bitcoin's long-term prospects.

Hougan suggested Bitcoin's market capitalisation could eventually reach $30 trillion, drawing comparisons with gold's expansion following the introduction of exchange-traded funds.

Not finding the right stocks? Our AI's list of investor-grade stock picks for October just dropped »

Such an outcome would represent a substantial increase from Bitcoin's current market value of approximately $1.66 trillion, although the forecast remains speculative.

Corporate adoption continued this week, with Robinhood reportedly adding $25 million in Bitcoin to its balance sheet.

Meanwhile, US government-linked wallets transferred approximately $1 billion in Bitcoin on Thursday, following earlier transfers totalling $770 million. The purpose of the movements remains unclear.

The combination of institutional adoption and persistent leverage risks underscores Bitcoin's competing market forces.

While improved trading data may help investors identify crowded positions, analysts caution that another large-scale liquidation event remains possible.

For now, Bitcoin faces an immediate test around $85,000, with its longer-term recovery dependent on renewed demand and more stable market positioning.

Broader crypto prices were mostly lower early Sunday, based on the latest market snapshot.

World No. 2 cryptocurrency Ether rose 0.40% to $2,508.16.

World No. 3 cryptocurrency XRP fell 1.05% to $1.3961.

Solana declined 0.40% to $109.72, while BNB dropped 0.38% to $748.29.

Summary: Investing.com -- Bitcoin remained above $83,000 on Sunday, roughly 34% below its record high, as investors marked one year since a historic $19 billion cryptocurrency liquidation event.
Content: Investing.com -- Bitcoin remained above $83,000 on Sunday, roughly 34% below its record high, as investors marked one year since a historic $19 billion cryptocurrency liquidation event.

The world's largest cryptocurrency was trading at $83,062.8 as at 01:23 ET (05:23 GMT), having failed to recover its October 6, 2025, peak of $126,080.

The anniversary follows another volatile week in which Bitcoin fell to $80,308 before recovering towards $83,000, highlighting persistent concerns over leveraged trading.

On October 10, 2025, Bitcoin plunged from approximately $122,000 to $105,000 after President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs on Chinese imports.

The selloff triggered more than $19 billion in liquidations across cryptocurrency markets, affecting approximately 1.6 million trading accounts.

Analysts warn that the conditions behind the crash remain largely intact, particularly the widespread use of perpetual futures and heavily leveraged positions.

Mark Connors of Risk Dimensions said derivatives positioning continues to influence Bitcoin's short-term price movements, despite improvements in market transparency.

Recent positioning data suggests approximately $3.3 billion in Bitcoin short positions could face liquidation if prices climb towards $85,000, potentially accelerating any recovery.

Institutional demand has also weakened, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recording more than $700 million in outflows this week.

Despite the market's struggles, Bitwise Asset Management Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan remains optimistic about Bitcoin's long-term prospects.

Hougan suggested Bitcoin's market capitalisation could eventually reach $30 trillion, drawing comparisons with gold's expansion following the introduction of exchange-traded funds.

Such an outcome would represent a substantial increase from Bitcoin's current market value of approximately $1.66 trillion, although the forecast remains speculative.

Corporate adoption continued this week, with Robinhood reportedly adding $25 million in Bitcoin to its balance sheet.

Meanwhile, US government-linked wallets transferred approximately $1 billion in Bitcoin on Thursday, following earlier transfers totalling $770 million. The purpose of the movements remains unclear.

The combination of institutional adoption and persistent leverage risks underscores Bitcoin's competing market forces.

While improved trading data may help investors identify crowded positions, analysts caution that another large-scale liquidation event remains possible.

For now, Bitcoin faces an immediate test around $85,000, with its longer-term recovery dependent on renewed demand and more stable market positioning.

Broader crypto prices were mostly lower early Sunday, based on the latest market snapshot.

World No. 2 cryptocurrency Ether rose 0.40% to $2,508.16.

title: Bitcoin Ranges Near $83K as Traders Look to US Inflation Data
summary: October rate-hike odds have slumped, but analysts say Treasury yields at two-decade highs are still keeping a lid on risk appetite.
content:
Bitcoin inched higher on Monday, trading at $83,327, up 0.6% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The asset is still down 2.9% over the past week.

The cryptocurrency has "struggled against an increasingly challenging macroeconomic backdrop," Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, told Decrypt .

"Rising energy prices have reignited inflation concerns, pushing US Treasury yields higher and strengthening the dollar as investors reassess the Federal Reserve's interest-rate trajectory," she said. "Despite its reputation as a potential alternative store of value, recent price action suggests investors continue to treat Bitcoin predominantly as a risk asset rather than a reliable geopolitical hedge."

Traders see a 19.4% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the Fed's October 28 meeting, down from 22.1% a week ago and 42.5% a month ago, according to CME FedWatch. Prediction markets Polymarket and Myriad both put the odds of a hike at 17% (Disclaimer: Myriad is a prediction market developed by Decrypt 's parent company Dastan).

A shift in rate expectations should in principle support Bitcoin, Bitfire's Jade Shi said, but elevated long-term Treasury yields mean broader financial conditions have not fully eased. That helps explain why Bitcoin has held up without decisively clearing resistance, she said.

The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.24% and the 30-year yield at 5.60%, according to CNBC, having hit 52-week highs of 5.37% and 5.73% last week. Yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades, CoinShares head of research James Butterfill wrote on Thursday.

Butterfill argued that if those yields increasingly reflect concerns about U.S. public finances rather than stronger growth, Bitcoin begins to look "less like a conventional risk asset and more like an alternative to government-issued money."

Digital asset fund flows have lost momentum after $11.1 billion of inflows since mid-July, according to CoinShares.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs drew $21.13 million in net inflows on Friday, after outflows of $487.07 million on Wednesday and $244.13 million on Thursday, according to SoSoValue.

Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana ETFs All in the Red for October

Technically, Bitcoin has been trading mainly between about $80,300 and $87,100, according to Bitfire. A break above $85,600 on stronger volume could open the way toward $87,395, while a drop below $82,000 would raise the risk of a move toward $79,000.

"The recent easing of Middle East tensions has provided some breathing room, but the sustainability of the rebound will depend on whether the improvement in sentiment translates into a more meaningful retreat in bond yields and the dollar," Hathorn said. "Attention now turns towards upcoming US inflation data, which could prove decisive in shaping expectations for the Fed's next move."

title: Bitcoin Tests Average Buyer’s Break-Even As ETF Outflows Clash With Wall Street Buying
summary: Darkfost said the market was oscillating around the $80,500 line in a pattern resembling late 2025 and early 2026, with the level holding as support for now.
content:
Bitcoin traded almost flat on Saturday, hovering just above $82,900.

CryptoQuant Darkfost analyst described this level as the average holder's break-even point.

On Wall Street, Fidelity's FBTC bought $354.1 million of Bitcoin over 20 trading days while Morgan Stanley added 92 coins this week to reach 10,639 BTC.

Bitcoin (BTC) traded flat on Saturday, sitting just above the price at which the average holder was neither up nor down, as one analyst said the setup looked like a repeat of a pattern from late last year.

That line sat around $80,500, according to CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost. It was the cost basis of all Bitcoin in circulation, weighted by how much money went into each purchase, so when the price hovered there, the market as a whole was roughly breaking even.

Darkfost said Bitcoin was oscillating around the break-even line in a pattern that resembled late 2025 and early 2026. A market sitting on that line created doubt, he said, which pushed investors to act. For now, it was holding as support.

Analyst Ted Pillows was watching slightly higher. A weekly close above $82,700 would mean buyers are in control, he said, and could open a move toward $87,000 to $88,000.

Bitcoin's price was trading at around $82,900, up by 0.3% at the time of writing. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BTC remained in the 'bearish' zone, while chatter around it stayed at 'low' levels over the past day.

Two of the largest names on Wall Street have kept adding while the price has gone sideways. Fidelity's FBTC fund bought $354.1 million of Bitcoin over the past 20 trading days, according to Arkham. Its other crypto funds bought in the same window, taking in $66.6 million of Ethereum (ETH) and $18.2 million of Solana (SOL). Morgan Stanley (MS) also added about 92 coins this week through its MSBT fund, Arkham data showed, lifting its total to 10,639 BTC worth roughly $880 million.

Those two funds were buying even as the broader ETF category bled money this week. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $487.07 million on Wednesday, and another $244.13 million on Thursday, according to SoSoValue data. A $21.13 million inflow on Friday recovered a fraction of it.

title: Why Bitcoin Can Fall Before a Fed Rate Hike, Then Rally After It Happens
summary: Bitcoin fell on rate hike rumors, then rallied after the Fed acted. Learn why markets price the future and how crypto fits into the investment mix.
content:
Wall Street has an old saying: buy the rumor, sell the news. Bitcoin seems to be doing the opposite in 2026. It took a beating this September as traders bet on a Fed rate hike, then rallied once the Fed actually pulled the trigger. Sounds backward, but it makes more sense than it looks.

The answer lies in how markets price the future and how Bitcoin fits into the investment mix. Rate hikes reshape the competition for investor dollars, and crypto has a complicated relationship with risk. Let's break down the moving parts.

Every investor is shopping around. When rates rise, Treasury bonds, savings accounts and CDs start paying more, and a guaranteed yield suddenly looks a lot better than an asset that pays nothing. Bitcoin doesn't generate interest or dividends. Its only payoff is the price going up, which makes it a tougher sell when the alternatives get more generous.

Higher rates also tend to weigh on risk assets like stocks and crypto. Bitcoin was pitched by some as a hedge against market turmoil, but its track record looks more like a traditional risk asset. In a Federal Reserve speech on crypto and financial stability, then-Vice Chair Lael Brainard said crypto assets had shown a high correlation with riskier stocks and overall investor risk appetite.

In plain terms, when stocks get jittery over expensive money, Bitcoin usually gets jittery right along with them.

Markets hate uncertainty more than they hate bad news. When rumors started swirling this summer that the Fed might have to hike, risk assets sold off. Bitcoin, being as volatile as it is, took a particularly hard hit.

Then the Fed actually moved. On Sept. 16, it raised its target range by a quarter of a percentage point, its first increase in more than three years. Bitcoin didn't collapse. By the next morning, CoinDesk reported that it had climbed modestly above $76,000.

The explanation is simple. Much of the bad news was already priced in, and the hike wasn't worse than expected. Attention quickly shifted to what the Fed would do next. The Fed's September projections pointed to only limited additional increases, which eased fears of a string of aggressive hikes. Bitcoin responded with a relief rally.

The same logic shows up when you look at a different stretch of the year. In July, some market participants were bracing for a rate hike, then inflation came in cooler than expected. In reaction to this news on July 15, Bitcoin jumped about 3.6%, per CoinDesk .

The mechanics ran in reverse. When investors think rates are less likely to rise, safe income-producing assets lose some of their pull, and riskier assets like Bitcoin get breathing room.

Rate expectations are a major driver, but not the only one. Supply and demand, geopolitical events, ETF flows, regulation and crypto-specific news all shape the price. And often, what traders expect matters more than what actually happens.

Bitcoin's reaction to Fed policy is a useful reminder that prices move on expectations long before the official announcement. If you're watching the Fed to time your crypto moves, you're not alone, but you're competing with a lot of people who are doing the same thing. Before you bet on the next rate decision, make sure your position still makes sense if the Fed does the opposite of what you expect.

title: Bitcoin’s Price Prediction: Will Global M2 Point to $300,000?
summary: A chart circulating in crypto circles claims global money supply points to Bitcoin hitting $250,000 to $300,000, and prominent voices are taking it seriously. But the math behind it hides a flaw that lets anyone bend the prediction to fit whatever outcome they want.
content:
Bitcoin trades at $82,965, down 5.3% in 2026, yet a viral global M2 chart predicts prices between $250,000 and $300,000.

The chart's time-lag is chosen subjectively using past data, making it appear accurate in hindsight while offering no genuine predictive power.

Bill Barhydt cited a speaker's claim that Bitcoin must reach $300,000 within 24 months, which stands as the article's only concrete, testable prediction.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is trading at $82,965 as of October 11, 2026, down 5.3% so far this year. Yet, a frequently shared global M2 Bitcoin chart circulating in crypto discussions posits a much higher potential price.

Bill Barhydt, CEO of the crypto firm Abra, recently referenced this chart on The Pomp Podcast . He stated, "If you look at the charts that everybody likes to show with global M2 versus Bitcoin, they're all saying Bitcoin should be around 250 to 300k-ish in that range," in an episode aired on October 8.

Many who share this chart may not fully understand what it measures or how it was constructed. So, can the amount of money in the world really indicate where Bitcoin's price is headed?

M2 measures how much money exists in an economy, including cash, checking accounts, and easily accessible savings like money market funds. The global M2 aggregates these figures across major economies, providing a rough estimate of the total money available worldwide.

The chart that often gets shared compares this global total with Bitcoin's price. Most versions of the chart adjust the money supply line forward by a certain number of weeks, based on the belief that newly created money takes time to flow through banks and markets before reaching riskier assets like cryptocurrencies.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

------

This approach has its charm. Bitcoin has a capped supply, meaning if the money supply—dollars, euros, and yuan—keeps rising while Bitcoin's supply remains fixed, each coin should, theoretically, become more valuable. Simon Dixon echoed this view on The Pomp Podcast , commending Bitcoin for having "a monetary policy which you can rely upon with a fixed supply."

However, choosing the money supply line is subjective. Changing the number of weeks in the shift alters the chart's suggested "fair" price for Bitcoin, so the prediction can change whenever the creator adjusts the timeframe.

First, while some correlations may hold, they don't explain why this new money is flowing into Bitcoin rather than other assets like stocks or gold. For instance, U.S. M2, a significant portion of the global total, hit a new peak in August, yet Bitcoin is down 5.3% this year.

Jordi Visser offered one perspective on this potential connection on September 19's episode of The Pomp Podcast . He suggested Bitcoin often trades on liquidity, since its real-world use hasn't fully emerged yet. If true, the connection between money supply and Bitcoin's price might weaken as other factors take over.

Second, chart creators often select the forward shift after analyzing past data. They can test different time lags against historical prices and choose the one that aligns best, making the chart look accurate in hindsight while offering little insight into future movements.

Most critically, this overlay creates a price target that lacks a set timeline. This makes it unfalsifiable; no outcome can definitively prove it wrong since proponents can always argue that the price hasn't reached the predicted level yet.

To his credit, Barhydt didn't claim any specificity in his prediction. He said this price range "feels right to me based upon where the markets are going," indicating judgment rather than a precise calculation.

He also quoted a speaker from a treasury conference, without claiming the view as his own: "if bitcoin's not at 300k in 24 months, then my thesis on Bitcoin was completely wrong." This statement is testable because it provides a specific timeframe for evaluation.

However, those promoting the chart in this discussion have not published a track record, making it hard for readers to gauge how often their predictions align with reality. Treat any claims about its accuracy with skepticism unless the authors present both successful predictions and misses.

While money supply illustrates the liquidity around Bitcoin, it doesn't provide a clear price forecast. An increasing money supply can lift risky assets, but the global M2 chart lets its creator dictate the lag and set a price target without a deadline. It also fails to outline the path from $82,965 to $300,000, which would require new capital to flow into Bitcoin rather than stocks or gold within a specified timeframe.

The dated 24-month claim presents the clearest opportunity for evaluation. Readers can assess Bitcoin's price 24 months following Barhydt's October 8 episode. If it hasn't touched $300,000 by that time, the conference speaker has already said the thesis was wrong. Furthermore, if the chart's forward shift subtly changes after a mismatch occurs, it's likely being adjusted post-hoc to fit Bitcoin's price.

Smaller coins, with less trading volume, can drop sharply on similar sell orders because fewer buyers are available at different price points.

NEAR's performance over the past month complicates this analysis. The blockchain network, designed for running applications, has surged 91.7% over the last 30 days, a stretch that includes the selloff week. This sharp rise may suggest earlier investors are still in profit, so a flat week could simply be a pause after recent gains.

Monero, known for privacy features that obscure transaction details, has risen 8.4% over the last month. Its more modest performance compared to NEAR weakens the momentum argument for its stable week, though price data alone can't rule out lighter trading activity.

Examining fund flows offers additional insight, though data is limited to five coins on the list. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) allow investors to own a coin through regular brokerage accounts. On October 8, Bitcoin-based funds lost $244 million, Ethereum funds lost $73 million, and Solana funds dropped $3.3 million. In contrast, XRP funds gained $8.2 million, and Dogecoin saw no change in flows.

Although these fund flows can inform us about investor sentiment, they don't always correlate neatly with price changes. For instance, XRP funds attracted new investment while XRP fell 9.0%, more than Bitcoin, which saw the largest outflow. Notably, there is no fund flow data for NEAR or Monero, so it's challenging to determine whether investor interest is supporting these coins.

Bitcoin performed well, dropping only 3.6% amid a turbulent market, even as $244 million left Bitcoin funds in a single day. While NEAR and Monero posted smaller losses, those results could reflect lower trading volume rather than genuine buying support.

Future market shifts will be critical to assessing NEAR and Monero's resilience. If Bitcoin drops below $80,000 and NEAR and Monero fall more sharply, their previous stability was likely due to lower trading volumes. However, if these coins remain stable while Bitcoin continues to slide, it would indicate healthy demand for NEAR and Monero and could position them as strong market contenders.

title: Bitcoin Has Closed Four Straight Weeks Above Its 50-Week Average. The Last Time It Did That It Tripled Within a Year.
summary: A rare pattern in Bitcoin's price history has only appeared twice before, and each time it triggered a dramatic move in completely opposite directions. Which outcome the current streak mirrors could define the next year for Bitcoin holders.
content:
Bitcoin has closed above its 50-week average ($76,618) for four straight weeks, trading at $83,369 as of October 12, 2026.

The last two times this signal triggered, Bitcoin surged 217% in 2023 but crashed 50% after an initial 170% gain in 2019.

A weekly close below $76,618 would end the streak and signal a return to a downtrend, making each week's close critical to watch.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has closed above its 50-week average for four straight weeks. As of October 12, 2026, Bitcoin is trading at $83,369, while its 50-week average sits at $76,618. If it closes below this average, it would end this current streak.

This indicator has appeared twice in the last decade, each time producing very different outcomes. In January 2023, Bitcoin climbed above the average near $23,000 and rose 217% to a high of around $73,000 by March 2024. Conversely, in April 2019, it rebounded to near $5,000 and initially surged 170% to about $13,800 by June, but then fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December of that same year.

So what does a fourth consecutive weekly close above the average suggest about what might happen next for Bitcoin holders?

The 50-week average is calculated by averaging Bitcoin's closing prices for the past 50 weeks. It helps smooth out price fluctuations, giving a clearer picture of longer-term trends. When Bitcoin stays above this average, it indicates that buyers are dominating the market. If it trades below, it suggests sellers are in control.

The 'weekly close' refers to the last price at the end of each trading week. Traders typically regard this price as more significant than daily closes because it reduces market noise. Since Bitcoin is traded around the clock, a sudden price spike on a single day can briefly push the price above or below the average before reverting back. A weekly close counts only if Bitcoin is above the line when the week ends.

When Bitcoin achieves four consecutive weekly closes above this average, it sets a higher standard. A single close might be a temporary bounce, but four consecutive ones show buyers have consistently held the price up.

The 2023 signal is often touted as a success story. When Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week average near $23,000 in January 2023, it skyrocketed 217% to roughly $73,000 by March 2024. Those who interpreted this signal as the start of a new uptrend were vindicated.

In contrast, the 2019 signal began similarly. After regaining the average near $5,000 in April 2019, it rose to about $13,800 by June—a significant increase. However, this rally was short-lived: Bitcoin fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December, leaving those who held through the year disappointed.

Analysts attribute these differences to factors like liquidity, the amount of money flowing into riskier investments, and the timing of halving events, when the rate of new Bitcoin production is reduced. However, with only two instances to reference, these explanations remain speculative.

Bitcoin is currently about 33.9% below its record high of $126,080. It has risen 8.0% over the past 30 days but fallen 3.2% in the last week. This mix of trends could indicate a scenario similar to either of the previous signals.

The 50-week average is always changing. Each week, the oldest closing price drops out of the calculation while the most recent price is included, slightly altering the average Bitcoin needs to maintain.

This four-week streak strongly suggests Bitcoin's trend may be shifting upward. However, it doesn't necessarily indicate how far the price will rise or how long this trend will last. Both past signals preceded significant gains, but one of those gains was largely lost by the year's end.

For now, holders should pay close attention. A weekly close below the average, currently around $76,618, would end the streak and suggest a shift back towards a downtrend. Until then, either a repeat of the 2023 rally or a downturn like 2019 remains possible.
